activities.name: Cabot’s Matthew
activities.region: Bristol and the eastern coast of North America
activities.note: Cabot sailed from Bristol in May. The Toby chronicle dates the landing to June 24 and the Bristol return to August 6. The departure day and the location of the eastern North American landing are unresolved.

activities.name: Cabot’s second fleet
activities.note: A London chronicle records an early May departure. In a July 25 dispatch, Pedro de Ayala reported that one damaged ship had reached an unidentified Irish port. The report does not describe the movements of Cabot or the rest of the fleet.

activities.name: Alonso Niño and Cristóbal Guerra
activities.note: A separately documented voyage reached pearl-producing areas along the northern South American coast.

activities.name: Ojeda, de la Cosa and Vespucci
activities.note: The expedition visited the coast of northern South America. This entry describes the documented 1499–1500 voyage. Other voyages attributed to Vespucci have separate evidentiary issues.

activities.name: Vicente Yáñez Pinzón’s Atlantic voyage
activities.note: The expedition crossed the South Atlantic and visited the coast of Brazil and the Amazon region. Exact first landfall is not assigned here.

activities.name: Gaspar Corte-Real’s first voyage
activities.note: The Cantino map’s legend associates this voyage with an ice-bound coast usually identified as Greenland. Its day dates, landing and precise sighting location remain unresolved.

activities.name: Gaspar Corte-Real’s second voyage
activities.region: North Atlantic and eastern North America
activities.note: Two ships returned to Lisbon after the expedition sailed along an unidentified North American coast and kidnapped Indigenous people. The third vessel, with Gaspar aboard, did not return.

activities.name: Miguel Corte-Real’s search
activities.region: North Atlantic and eastern North America
activities.note: Góis gives May 10 for the Lisbon departure. An August 20 rendezvous is reported, but its North American location is disputed. Two vessels returned and Miguel’s ship was never heard from again.

activities.name: Balboa crosses the Isthmus of Panama
activities.note: Balboa’s party crossed Indigenous territories to the Pacific coast. Evidence supports the year. Exact summit and shore days remain uncertain.

activities.name: Ponce de León’s 1513 Florida voyage
activities.note: The record places Ponce de León on the Florida coast in April. Exact landfall location and the full sequence of the coastal voyage require separate treatment.

activities.name: Cortés’s expedition from Cuba
activities.region: Gulf of Mexico and central Mexico
activities.note: The Spanish expedition reached the Gulf coast and began the inland campaign in 1519. Indigenous diplomacy, alliances and resistance shaped the routes.

activities.name: Ponce de León’s return to Florida
activities.note: Ponce de León returned in a colonization attempt, was wounded during Indigenous resistance and withdrew to Cuba.

activities.name: Cabeza de Vaca and fellow survivors
activities.note: Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, Andrés Dorantes, Alonso del Castillo and Estevanico survived the Narváez expedition and reached Spanish settlements in 1536. Details and identifications along the route remain contested.

activities.name: Narváez’s Florida expedition
activities.note: The expedition landed near Tampa Bay and moved through Indigenous territories before departing in improvised craft.

activities.name: Cartier’s Stadacona winter
activities.note: Cartier’s party wintered on the Saint-Charles River. Iroquoians showed the crew a remedy for scurvy. An exact return date from Hochelaga is omitted in the route.

activities.name: De Soto’s expedition in the Southeast
activities.note: De Soto led a Spanish expedition through Indigenous homelands from Florida to the Mississippi region. This band ends with de Soto’s death. A separate band describes the survivors.

activities.name: Coronado’s expedition
activities.region: Northern New Spain and North American Southwest
activities.note: Coronado’s parties traveled through Pueblo homelands and east toward the Great Plains. The expedition split into branches with distinct routes.

activities.name: Moscoso and the de Soto expedition survivors
activities.note: Survivors continued under Luis de Moscoso, then withdrew by the Mississippi and Gulf of Mexico.

activities.name: Roberval’s St. Lawrence expedition
activities.note: Roberval continued from Newfoundland to Cap-Rouge in 1542. The surviving colonists were repatriated in 1543. Cap-Rouge arrival is reported to the month.

activities.name: Frobisher’s first Baffin Island leg
activities.note: The Gabriell continued to Baffin Island and investigated the waters now called Frobisher Bay. The surviving chronology does not yield a precise route here.

activities.name: Frobisher’s second Arctic voyage
activities.note: The expedition returned to the Frobisher Bay area to extract mineral ore. Accounts describe conflict and Inuit captives taken to England.

activities.name: Frobisher’s third Arctic voyage
activities.note: A larger mining fleet returned to Arctic waters. The expedition did not establish the planned settlement.

activities.name: John Davis’s second Northwest Passage voyage
activities.note: A new voyage returned to western Greenland and the Davis Strait region. Separate ship movements are not reconstructed.

activities.name: John Davis’s third Northwest Passage voyage
activities.note: Davis returned to west Greenland and explored further north before returning to England.

activities.name: Dugua de Mons and Champlain in Acadia
activities.note: The group tried a settlement on Île Sainte-Croix, moved to Port-Royal, and surveyed parts of the Atlantic coast before the operation ended.

activities.name: Hudson’s Discovery · James Bay winter
activities.note: Discovery became icebound in November. The precise berth is uncertain. The full dated ship route resumes with documented homeward movement in June.

activities.name: Bylot and Baffin’s first Discovery voyage
activities.note: Bylot commanded and Baffin piloted on an earlier voyage, separate from their 1616 survey.

activities.name: Jolliet and Marquette’s downstream journey
activities.note: The party traveled farther south and turned back in July. The precise turnaround date is omitted here.

activities.name: Mackenzie’s return from the Beaufort Sea
activities.note: The party resumed the upstream journey in July and reached its original post in September. Dated examples include the Liard confluence, the entrance to Great Slave Lake and portages along the Slave River.

activities.name: Mackenzie’s return from the Pacific
activities.region: Nuxalk–Carrier Grease Trail, Fraser and Peace rivers
activities.note: The party returned along the Indigenous trade corridor and recovered the canoe it had cached near the Fraser before the westward crossing. It reached the Peace River departure post on August 24.

activities.name: Zebulon Pike’s Southwest expedition
activities.region: U.S. interior and northern New Spain
activities.note: Pike led the U.S. government expedition into the southern Great Plains and the Rocky Mountains. Surviving maps and papers document the field campaign.

activities.name: Bransfield and Smith’s Antarctic Peninsula survey
activities.region: South Shetland Islands and Antarctic Peninsula
activities.note: The expedition reported an Antarctic Peninsula sighting on 30 January, with the coastal identification set out in the historical research.

activities.name: Nathaniel Palmer’s Antarctic Peninsula observations
activities.note: Palmer’s November report is one of several early Antarctic sighting accounts. Its place in priority arguments remains a separate question.

activities.name: Dumont d’Urville’s Antarctic survey
activities.note: The French expedition observed the coast and recovered geological samples. Offshore encounters and landing evidence are distinguishable.

activities.name: John C. Frémont’s western survey
activities.note: A U.S. government expedition surveyed routes to Oregon, across the Great Basin and onward to California. Archival route materials distinguish this expedition from the other Frémont parties.

activities.name: McClure’s Investigator expedition
activities.note: McClure’s party entered from the Pacific, became icebound, transferred across the ice and returned with a different vessel. The band covers the expedition including its relief and return.

activities.name: Qitdlarssuaq and Inuit families’ migration
activities.region: Qikiqtaaluk, Ellesmere Island and northwest Greenland
activities.note: Inuit community histories describe families traveling north from the Mittimatalik region. Historical and oral sources place the movement in the 1850s and early 1860s. This broad interval preserves that precision.

activities.name: Rae’s Boothia survey and Franklin evidence
activities.region: Repulse Bay, Boothia, Pelly Bay and western Hudson Bay
activities.note: Rae’s mission was a coastal survey. Inuit travelers supplied information about Franklin’s lost crews and sold relics at Pelly Bay and Repulse Bay. The land and boat routes belong to Rae’s party; no route for Franklin’s survivors is inferred.

activities.name: McClintock and Hobson’s Fox expedition
activities.note: The search recovered a surviving note on King William Island, alongside Inuit testimony and additional expedition traces.

activities.name: De Long’s Jeannette expedition
activities.note: Jeannette entered from the Pacific side and became beset in Arctic pack ice. The crew abandoned the ship after it was crushed in 1881.

activities.name: Greely’s Lady Franklin Bay expedition
activities.region: Ellesmere Island and western Greenland approaches
activities.note: The expedition established a research station at Fort Conger, withdrew south, and was reached by a relief party in 1884.

activities.name: Sverdrup’s second Fram expedition
activities.note: The ship wintered around Ellesmere Island and supported extensive sledge surveys. The date band does not reconstruct the winter bases’ individual movement histories.

activities.name: Drygalski’s Gauss expedition
activities.region: Indian Ocean sector of East Antarctica
activities.note: The first German Antarctic expedition wintered beset in sea ice and surveyed the region later named Kaiser Wilhelm II Land.

activities.name: Charcot’s Français expedition
activities.note: The first French expedition under Charcot conducted hydrographic and scientific work and overwintered in the Antarctic Peninsula region.

activities.name: Gjøa at King Point
activities.note: Gjøa spent its third Arctic winter here. Amundsen traveled inland from the winter base. Sources differ on when the ship resumed its voyage, so this band stops before the earliest reported resumption.

activities.name: Frederick Cook’s Arctic expedition
activities.note: Cook claimed in 1909 to have reached the North Pole in April 1908. The claim is disputed and has no mapped pole waypoint.

activities.name: Charcot’s Pourquoi-Pas? expedition
activities.note: The second French Antarctic expedition extended coastal surveying farther south and west of the earlier fieldwork.

activities.name: Peary, Henson and Inuit expedition members
activities.note: The party conducted an attempt on the North Pole. Peary’s claim of reaching it in April 1909 remains disputed and has no mapped pole waypoint.

activities.name: Shirase’s Kainan Maru expedition
activities.region: Ross Sea and Ross Ice Shelf
activities.note: The Japanese expedition used Sydney as a staging point and reached Antarctic waters and the Ross Ice Shelf during the 1911–1912 season.

activities.name: Filchner’s Deutschland expedition
activities.note: The second German Antarctic expedition explored the southern Weddell Sea and wintered beset in the pack. The vessel escaped the ice in 1912.

activities.name: Australasian Antarctic Expedition · field seasons
activities.note: After the deployment to Cape Denison, field parties worked at multiple bases. Mawson and others remained for a second winter before the final evacuation.

activities.name: Aurora’s Ross Sea pack drift
activities.note: Aurora tore away from its moorings and drifted north while depot-laying members remained ashore. The damaged vessel eventually reached New Zealand.

activities.name: Southern Sky · first Endurance rescue attempt
activities.note: Shackleton left South Georgia on 23 May. Pack ice prevented Southern Sky from reaching Elephant Island.

activities.name: Instituto de Pesca No. 1 · second Endurance rescue attempt
activities.note: Uruguay lent its survey ship for the June rescue attempt. It approached Elephant Island but could not proceed through the ice.

activities.name: Emma · third Endurance rescue attempt
activities.note: Emma sailed from Punta Arenas in July. Storm and ice forced it back. Yelcho later made the successful rescue on a separate voyage.

activities.name: Amundsen and Sverdrup’s Maud expedition
activities.note: The expedition sailed the Northeast Passage and made separate years of Arctic drift and scientific observations. Leadership and activity changed within the band.

activities.name: Fifth Thule Expedition
activities.region: Greenland, Canadian Arctic, Alaska and Chukotka
activities.note: Rasmussen, Arnarulunnguaq, Qaavigarsuaq and fellow team members documented travel and life in Inuit communities. The whole-expedition band has no inferred daily path.

activities.name: Ellsworth’s first Antarctic flight attempt
activities.note: The expedition was unable to complete the flight plan after its aircraft was damaged on pack ice in early 1934.

activities.name: Ellsworth’s second Antarctic flight attempt
activities.note: The 1934 season was a new attempt. The completed transcontinental flight occurred in 1935, beyond this atlas’s endpoint.

activities.name: Rodrigo de Bastidas and Juan de la Cosa
activities.region: Caribbean coasts of present-day Colombia and Panama; Hispaniola
activities.note: The expedition followed the coast past the Magdalena and Gulf of Urabá toward Darién before damaged vessels reached Hispaniola. The source labels it 1501–02 but gives a June 1500 departure in the text. The band spans this disagreement.

activities.name: Vespucci’s voyage in Portuguese service
activities.region: South Atlantic and Atlantic coast of South America
activities.note: The voyage of 1501–02 has stronger evidence than the 1497–98 voyage attributed to Vespucci. Reported southern limits and modern place identifications remain disputed.

activities.name: Voyage attributed to Vespucci in 1497
activities.note: The itinerary attributed to Vespucci for 1497–98 depends on disputed letter evidence. These are the claimed years.

activities.name: Díaz de Solís and the Río de la Plata expedition
activities.region: Atlantic, southern Brazil, Río de la Plata and Andalusia
activities.note: Three ships sailed from Sanlúcar and explored the estuary. Sources differ on the month and sequence of the estuary landings and Solís’s death. Survivors returned by the Brazilian coast, where part of the expedition was stranded.

activities.name: Hernández de Córdoba along the Gulf coast
activities.note: After the encounter near Cabo Catoche, the expedition continued along the Yucatán coast to Campeche and Champotón, where Maya defenders inflicted severe losses. The wounded expedition withdrew toward Cuba. Dates of intermediate coastal movements differ between sources.

activities.name: Grijalva’s Gulf coast reconnaissance and return
activities.region: Cozumel, Campeche, Tabasco, Veracruz and Cuba
activities.note: Grijalva’s expedition fought at Champotón and surveyed Boca de Términos. It continued to the Sacrificios and San Juan de Ulúa area. Alvarado detached to return to Cuba. The complete westward track and the separate return sailings need more precise anchors.

activities.name: Cortés’s retreat and the siege of Tenochtitlan
activities.note: Cortés’s group retreated from Tenochtitlan on 30 June 1520. His forces, together with an Indigenous coalition, later besieged and captured the city on 13 August 1521. The coastal route and 1519 advance are shown separately.

activities.name: Narváez’s Apalachee and Bay of Horses phases
activities.region: Apalachee and northern Gulf of Mexico coast
activities.note: The force occupied settlements, faced Indigenous resistance, moved toward Aute and built five improvised boats at the Bay of Horses. It set out on 22 September. The precise locations of Aute and the embarkation site need further verification.

activities.name: De Soto’s winter at Anhaica
activities.note: The expedition occupied the Apalachee capital over the winter, consuming local stores and relying on forced labor. Archaeology identifies the site. The dated itinerary anchors the 3 March departure.

activities.name: Coronado’s Tiguex winter and war
activities.region: Tiguex Pueblo region, Middle Rio Grande
activities.note: Coronado’s expedition wintered in Tiguex. The expedition’s demands and violence led to war, deaths and the displacement of Pueblo communities. Coronado left east toward Quivira on 23 April 1541. Pueblo and route identifications remain approximate.

activities.name: Coronado’s Quivira detachment
activities.region: Rio Grande, Southern Plains and Wichita country
activities.note: The army left Tiguex on 23 April. A smaller force continued northeast to Quivira with Plains guides after Coronado sent most of the army back. He returned to the Rio Grande region in September. The details of the Plains itinerary and exact arrival day remain unresolved.

activities.name: Alvarado, Tovar and Cárdenas scouting parties
activities.region: Acoma, Tiguex and Cicuye; Hopi communities and Grand Canyon
activities.note: Hernando de Alvarado left Zuni on 29 August for Acoma, Tiguex and Cicuye. Pedro de Tovar went toward Hopi communities, while García López de Cárdenas traveled to the canyon. These are distinct parties. The dates and sites required for detailed tracks are uneven.

activities.name: Eliza and Alberni winter at Nootka Sound
activities.note: The Spanish contingent rebuilt at Yuquot with the agreement of Maquinna as described in the sources. Wet weather, spoiled supplies and scurvy strained the 1790–91 winter. Eliza then renewed survey work in 1791.

activities.name: Roberval at France-Roy and repatriation
activities.note: The colony occupied Cartier’s former fort from late July 1542. After a difficult winter and exploration toward the Ottawa River, the group abandoned the colony and returned to France in early September 1543.

activities.name: Frobisher’s mining camp and attempted settlement
activities.note: The damaged fleet gathered near the mining site at the end of July. The fleet repaired ships and loaded ore, while the intended winter colony was dropped after supplies were lost.

activities.name: Basque whaling in the Strait of Belle Isle
activities.region: Red Bay, Labrador and Strait of Belle Isle
activities.note: Basque crews made repeated fishing and whaling voyages, processing whales at coastal stations. The Red Bay wreck is provisionally identified as the San Juan, reportedly lost in 1565. The band covers the general sixteenth-century whaling period.

activities.name: Davis’s detached Sunshine and North Star
activities.note: Sunshine and North Star were sent to search for a northward passage between Greenland and Iceland. The attempt was blocked by ice and North Star was lost in a storm.

activities.name: Davis’s detached fishing barks
activities.note: Elizabeth and Sunshine separated from Davis’s pinnace on June 21 to fish. Their subsequent courses and reunion or return dates require separate evidence.

activities.name: Franklin’s first winter at Beechey Island
activities.note: The chronology of the 1845–46 winter relies on the camp, records and burials. Those sources substantiate the base. The ship-arrival and departure days remain unestablished.

activities.name: Investigator’s first winter in Prince of Wales Strait
activities.region: Prince of Wales Strait near Princess Royal Islands
activities.note: Investigator froze into the strait. Sledge parties explored adjoining shores and demonstrated an opening into Viscount Melville Sound. After the ice released the ship, it withdrew and sailed around the west side of Banks Island.

activities.name: Bedford Pim’s first Investigator relief journey
activities.region: Dealy Island, Viscount Melville Sound and Mercy Bay
activities.note: Pim and his companions crossed the frozen sound by sledge from Kellett’s expedition at Dealy Island. They reached Investigator on April 6.

activities.name: Investigator crew at Beechey Island and return to England
activities.region: Viscount Melville Sound, Beechey Island, Greenland and England
activities.note: Since both relief ships were beset, the crew traveled by sledge to Beechey Island. They returned to England on September 28 with the crews of the Belcher search expedition.

activities.name: Fram at Goose Fiord
activities.note: Fram used the fiord through the third and fourth winters, with nearby boat and sledging activities. Summer ice prevented a 1901 departure.

activities.name: Second Fram expedition’s parallel surveys
activities.region: Ellesmere, Axel Heiberg, Ringnes islands and north Devon Island
activities.note: Separate parties used the winter quarters to survey islands and fjords. Isachsen’s Ringnes traverse and Baumann’s Beechey Island journey have dated selections, while further inland survey points remain at broad seasonal precision.

activities.name: Tessem and Knudsen’s detached mail and records party
activities.region: Taymyr coast from Maudhavn toward Dikson
activities.note: The two men remained at the shore cabin when the ship departed on September 12. Their deaths and the discovery of remains are documented, while their last route and exact death locations remain uncertain.

activities.name: Harald Sverdrup’s winter journeys with Chukchi herders
activities.note: Sverdrup traveled with Chukchi participants through the winter, learned from them and returned to the ship on May 17. The route was separate from the Maud.

activities.name: Maud’s final winter off the Kolyma coast
activities.region: East Siberian Sea near the Medvezhyi Islands
activities.note: After leaving the main drift, the Maud was trapped once more off the Kolyma coast near Four Pillar Island. It escaped in the summer of 1925.

activities.name: Omdal and Amundsen’s Wainwright shore party
activities.note: The two aviators and equipment traveled separately from the Maud after the expedition split. Omdal wintered ashore. Two dated 1923 air tests mark the end of the intended trans-Arctic effort.

activities.name: Odd Dahl and Oscar Wisting’s Maud ice reconnaissance flights
activities.note: MiA’s archival chronology dates two short July 16 flights from ice near the ship, followed by a landing accident. The Fram Museum gives May for the pair of flights. Without precise fixes for the individual sorties, the aviation activity remains separate from the ship’s mapped track.

activities.name: Jolliet and Marquette’s Illinois River and Great Lakes return
activities.region: Mississippi, Illinois River, Illinois–Lake Michigan portage and Green Bay
activities.note: After leaving the Quapaw settlement area on July 17, the party paddled back upriver to the Illinois River. An Illinois chief and young men escorted them to Lake Michigan. Green Bay was reached in late September.

activities.name: Roberval at St. John’s before the St. Lawrence voyage
activities.note: The ships arrived on 8 June and remained until about the end of the month. The Canadian Museum of History dates departure to 30 June; the participant account uses an approximate month-end description.

activities.name: Antarctic survivors at Paulet Island
activities.note: Survivors built and occupied a stone hut until Uruguay retrieved the remaining group after Larsen’s party reached Snow Hill.

activities.name: Hope Bay party reunites with Nordenskjöld
activities.region: Hope Bay, Vega Island and Snow Hill Island
activities.note: The winter party left Hope Bay in late September, met Nordenskjöld at Vega Island on 12 October and reached Snow Hill later in October.

activities.name: Astrolabe and Zélée · Pacific and Aotearoa surveys
activities.region: Pacific Ocean and Aotearoa New Zealand
activities.note: The expedition’s main Pacific research separated the two southern seasons. Visits to Aotearoa in 1840 followed the second Antarctic voyage.

activities.name: Valdivia · Southern Ocean sampling
activities.note: The Antarctic survey formed part of a wider deep-sea expedition. Biological and oceanographic sampling continued on the passage toward Kerguelen.

activities.name: Gauss · Gaussberg and shore sledging
activities.region: Kaiser Wilhelm II Land and Davis Sea
activities.note: A March sledging party reached the volcanic cone now called Gaussberg. Further sledge outings and observations took place during 1902.

activities.name: Shirase expedition · Sydney winter
activities.note: The expedition established a camp and repaired Kainan Maru before the second Ross Sea voyage.

activities.name: Deutschland · Weddell Sea drift and ice work
activities.note: The ice carried the ship north with winter scientific work on the ice. A sledge party undertook a search for the reported Morrell Land and found no land at the presumed location.

activities.name: Frank Wild’s Western Base
activities.region: Shackleton Ice Shelf, Queen Mary Land
activities.note: Wild and seven companions spent one winter at a hut on floating ice. Their parties surveyed west toward Gaussberg and east toward Denman Glacier.

activities.name: Mawson’s party · second Cape Denison winter
activities.note: Members remained after the delayed return of the Far Eastern Party. Aurora recovered the remaining shore party in December.

activities.name: Ainsworth’s Macquarie Island wireless party
activities.note: The island party ran a scientific station and supplied the Cape Denison wireless link to Australia. Aurora collected the expedition party during its final voyage.

activities.name: BANZARE · second-season aerial survey
activities.region: Wilkes Land, Princess Elizabeth Land and Mac.Robertson Land
activities.note: Aircraft reconnaissance included Cape Goodenough and the Banzare Coast in January and Leopold and Astrid Coast, MacKenzie Bay and the Mac.Robertson Coast in February.

activities.name: Clerke’s final approach and change of command
activities.note: Clerke died at sea on 22 August. The ships reached Avacha Bay on 24 August, and Gore and King took their new commands on the 25th. The last selected ship fix under Clerke is 20 August; no fixed death coordinate is inferred.

activities.name: Columbus on Hispaniola, detention and return
activities.note: After the Paria voyage, Columbus returned to Hispaniola. Bobadilla removed him from office in 1500 and sent him to Spain in chains. The band includes that return; it is not a continuous occupation at one point.

activities.name: Columbus’s party stranded on Jamaica
activities.note: The ships reached Jamaica in June 1503 and the rescued party left on 28 June 1504. Puerto Bueno arrival, the later beaching at Santa Gloria and the eclipse are distinct events; the start of a particular beach stay is not assigned a day here.

activities.name: La Pérouse’s last passage and loss
activities.note: After the 10 March departure from Botany Bay, the ships were lost at Vanikoro during 1788. The wreck day and final sailing route are unknown; the year band does not mean the ships survived through December.

activities.name: Orellana’s detached upper-river party
activities.note: The detached party left Gonzalo Pizarro in December 1541 and continued downriver. Early camps and the competing upper-river geographical identifications are held; no exact mapped departure site is asserted. The dated route resumes at the Rio Negro confluence.

activities.name: Orellana’s second Amazon expedition
activities.region: Sanlúcar, Atlantic islands and Amazon estuary
activities.note: A distinct colonizing expedition sailed from Sanlúcar in May 1545, suffered severe losses, and ended with Orellana’s death and survivor withdrawals in the Amazon estuary. The 1542 river descent is not reused as its route.

activities.name: Champlain’s allied campaign and autumn hunting
activities.region: Wendat country, Lake Ontario and Haudenosaunee country
activities.note: Champlain accompanied Wendat and allied warriors toward an unsuccessful fortified-village attack, was wounded, and returned with his hosts after hunting and winter travel. Contested fort identifications and exact Lake Ontario crossings are not pinned.

activities.name: Champlain’s Wendat winter and Petun visits
activities.region: Wendat and Petun country, southern Georgian Bay
activities.note: Champlain stayed with Wendat hosts and visited neighboring Petun settlements. The edition has uncertain January/February labels and an editorial May inference for departure; this broad band does not manufacture a continuous stay at Cahiagué.

activities.name: Alarcón’s separate Colorado boat parties
activities.note: Two ascents began on 26 August and 14 September. The ships stayed in the delta while boats moved among river communities. The letter does not securely locate the upstream limit, villages or return days, so no daily river track is drawn.

activities.name: Chirikov’s St. Paul · separate voyage
activities.region: Kamchatka, Alaska and the Aleutian Islands
activities.note: The ship separated from Bering’s St. Peter in June. Selected observations do not recover its complete daily track; dates retain Old Style.

activities.name: Dementiev and ten companions · missing boat party
activities.region: Southeast Alaska, unidentified landing near the ship’s coastal survey
activities.note: Chirikov dates the boat’s dispatch to July 18. The date marks departure alone; the boat approached shore but never returned. No death date, subsequent route, secure landing or attack by Indigenous people is asserted.

activities.name: Savelev and three companions · second missing boat party
activities.note: Savelev, the carpenter, the calker and Fadiev went to assist Dementiev’s party. Neither boat returned. Their subsequent movements and fate remain unknown.

activities.name: Matonabbee, Hearne and companions · northern journey
activities.region: Hudson Bay, Coppermine River and Great Slave Lake
activities.note: Dated anchors mark departure, Arctic coast, Great Slave Lake and return. Travel through changing camps and communities remains geographically unresolved between them.

activities.name: Mistegan · detached coastal reconnaissance
activities.region: Western Boothia, north of Point de la Guiche
activities.note: Rae says Mistegan traveled six miles farther north and climbed rough ice to observe about five additional miles of coast. His precise endpoint is not fixed. This independent activity must remain visible alongside the main party.

activities.name: Vostok and Mirny · second Antarctic field season
activities.region: Macquarie Island, Pacific Southern Ocean and South Shetlands
activities.note: Selected journal-derived ship observations cover the southern cruise; intervening positions and date-line convention are qualified in the dated route.

activities.name: Étoile · repairs and separate homeward voyage
activities.note: Bougainville left Étoile careening at Mauritius and says it reached France a month after Boudeuse. His narrative gives only late-December departure and a relative return, so no exact-day route is supplied.

activities.name: Hoorn burned during careening
activities.note: The smaller ship caught fire while reeds were burned beneath her hull on 19 December. The account describes salvage on 20–21 December. Eendracht continued; this activity does not supply a surveyed wreck position.

activities.name: Pacific islands and New Guinea route awaiting place reconciliation
activities.region: Tuamotus, Tonga, Futuna, Bismarck Archipelago and New Guinea
activities.note: The first-person narrative gives numerous dated islands, encounters, provisioning attempts and violent confrontations. Several historical names and dead-reckoned positions require comparison with Le Maire’s independent journal and modern historical geography. The coarse dated Tafahi, Futuna and Ternate references do not substitute for a complete Pacific track.

activities.name: Seizure, calendar reconciliation and change of vessel
activities.note: The account dates seizure to 1 November by shipboard reckoning and 2 November locally, then records skipping a day. Schouten and Le Maire returned in Amsterdam. The OCR/printed transcription renders Le Maire’s death day as the impossible thirty-second of December; this pass does not invent a corrected death date or death-at-sea location.

activities.name: Storm-driven return through Fuegian channels
activities.region: Magellan Strait, Tierra del Fuego and the Pacific approaches
activities.note: The first Cape Pillar exit on 3 March failed in heavy weather. Slocum describes driving southeast and regaining the strait through Cockburn Channel before returning to St Nicholas Bay. Repeated attempts from Port Angosto ended with the successful departure on 13 April. His broad phrase about weathering Cape Horn is not encoded as a literal Cape Horn rounding.

activities.name: Juan Fernández to Samoa, with an undated Marquesas sighting
activities.note: Slocum describes lunar-distance work and sighting an island he calls Nukahiva, then later reaches Apia. The island is described as the southernmost Marquesas island, which does not match Nuku Hiva’s geography. Neither an exact day nor an unqualified modern island identification is invented.

activities.name: Bass Strait, Tasmania and a revised route through Torres Strait
activities.region: Southeastern Australia, Tasmania and the Great Barrier Reef
activities.note: Persistent bad weather led Slocum to abandon a westward route past Cape Leeuwin, visit Tasmania, and return north through the reef and Torres Strait. Dated harbour and channel anchors preserve that change; intermediate reef passages and undated Tasmanian calls remain gaps.

activities.name: Icelandic households settle in Greenland

activities.name: Norse work at L'Anse aux Meadows

activities.name: Trees cut at L'Anse aux Meadows in 1021
activities.note: Three trees with metal-tool modifications date to cutting in 1021. This fixes activity, not first arrival, a ship position or the identity of the workers.
